overview: This file documents Japanese tin production, processing, recycling, and trade between November 1934 and January 1937. Its principal records are Embassy despatches responding to State Department inquiries: a 1934 questionnaire on tin production and shipments, and a detailed 1936 investigation of Japan’s detinning industry, including plant capacities, scrap importers, production figures, and import-export statistics. Cross-reference sheets connect these reports with related material on Kyushu tin deposits, shipments to Japan, Siamese tin-restriction policy, and the Toa Kigyo Corporation’s Yokohama detinning plant. Collectively, the papers show Japan’s dependence on imported tinplate scrap—especially from the United States—alongside expectations that expanding domestic tinplate production and newly exploited deposits would support a more self-sufficient industry.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 1062 on Japanese tin production
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet refers researchers to despatch no. 1062 and its enclosed report on tin production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs the reader to decimal-file item 800.6354/52 for despatch no. 1062 from Grew in Japan. It identifies the subject as Japanese tin production and notes that a report was enclosed.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1062: Questionnaire for Tin Investigation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy submits a preliminary response to a congressional questionnaire concerning Japanese tin production.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to Department instruction no. 625 of October 11, 1934—the OCR misreads the year as 1884—requesting information for a House Foreign Affairs Committee subcommittee. He encloses a short report prepared from information supplied by the Commercial Attaché and states that a more detailed report will follow by later mail.

subfiles.title: Enclosed answers to the tin-investigation questionnaire
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, based on Commercial Attaché information
subfiles.about: This enclosure supplies brief figures and answers concerning tin shipments and an Osaka tin factory.
subfiles.summary: The report gives nine-month 1934 tin-ore shipments as 575 tons and records a June 1 shipment connected with New York. It describes a Japanese-owned Osaka tin factory with an annual output of 800 tons and associates it with International Tin Committee control. Although the page header reads November 17, 1936, its contents and attachment to despatch no. 1062 place it in 1934.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch no. 1886 on Japan’s detinning industry
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet points to a report on Japanese detinning companies, plant capacity, and expanding domestic tin production.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to another decimal-file location for the June 11, 1936 report; the OCR corrupts both the despatch number and date. It summarizes a combined factory capacity of 4,500 tons per month and attributes increased Japanese tin production to the opening of deposits in Kyushu.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1886: The Detinning Industry in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports on the scale, methods, raw materials, and products of Japanese detinning operations.
subfiles.summary: Responding to instruction no. 1029, the Embassy reports that listed factories could treat 4,500 tons of tin scrap monthly, although it could not determine how much tin they recovered. Japanese plants used chemical methods modeled on American practice and produced tin, tin tetrachloride for weighting silk, and reusable steel scrap. The report discusses Japan’s dependence on imported American tinplate scrap, the effects of the U.S. export prohibition, and the possibility that domestic tinplate production would eventually supply enough scrap for a wholly domestic industry. Pages 7 and 8 preserve duplicate OCR versions of the despatch’s second page, with page 8 being clearer.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 1: Companies detinning tin scrap
subfiles.about: This enclosure lists eight Tokyo and Osaka detinning factories and their estimated monthly consumption of tin scrap.
subfiles.summary: The list identifies four Tokyo-area and four Osaka-area operations, giving street addresses and capacities ranging from 200 to 1,500 tons per month. The entries total 4,500 tons monthly, with Osaka Refined Tin Works the largest listed plant at 1,500 tons.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 2: Importers of tin scrap
subfiles.about: This enclosure identifies Japanese firms importing tin scrap and supplies their Tokyo and, where applicable, New York addresses.
subfiles.summary: The list names Mitsui Bussan Kaisha, Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha, Iwai & Company, and a fourth importer whose OCR-corrupted name appears as “Lasakawa Kojire Hoton.” The first three firms have both Tokyo and New York addresses, illustrating the commercial channels connecting Japan’s detinning plants with American scrap supplies.

subfiles.title: Enclosure no. 3: Japanese Tin Statistics
subfiles.about: This enclosure tabulates Japanese tin production and trade from 1933 through partial-year 1936.
subfiles.summary: The table records production rising from 981.135 metric tons in 1933 to 2,059.669 tons in 1935, followed by 561.738 tons in the first three months of 1936. It also gives exports of tin ore and tin foil and imports of ingots, slabs, and chiefly scrap, showing that ingot and slab imports greatly exceeded domestic output.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Singapore despatch no. 57 on tin ore and Siam
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State filing system
subfiles.about: This sheet refers to a Singapore despatch concerning tin-ore shipments to Japan and speculation about Japanese influence on Siam’s tin policy.
subfiles.summary: The note directs readers to file 893.6354/40 for despatch no. 57 concerning a shipment of tin ore to Japan. It records local speculation that Japan might be influencing Siam’s attitude toward tin restriction, prompted by a statement from newly appointed Japanese Minister Itarō Ishii.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to E. Becker correspondence
subfiles.about: This damaged or badly OCR-corrupted sheet refers to December 1936 correspondence involving E. Becker and a Japanese subject that cannot be recovered reliably.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to a related 811.6354 file and identifies E. Becker as the sender. Most of the affiliation, recipient, and subject line is too garbled to establish the precise transaction, although the surviving fragment indicates that it concerned Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant
subfiles.about: This sheet refers to a memorandum containing J. T. Hashimoto’s information on the Toa Kigyo Corporation’s Yokohama plant and other Japanese detinning plants.
subfiles.summary: The note directs readers to an 811.6354 memorandum filed under “Allotments–Boston Can Co./19.” It identifies the subject as the Toa Kigyo Corporation detinning plant in Yokohama and comparable plants elsewhere in Japan, based on information supplied by J. T. Hashimoto.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference to memorandum on the Toa Kigyo detinning plant
subfiles.about: This is a duplicate copy of the cross-reference to the memorandum about Toa Kigyo’s Yokohama detinning plant.
subfiles.summary: The sheet duplicates page 14’s filing reference, date, sender, recipient, and subject. It again attributes the information about the Yokohama and other Japanese detinning plants to J. T. Hashimoto of the Toa Kigyo Corporation.

interest: The file is especially valuable for its unusually granular industrial evidence: it names individual factories and scrap importers, supplies addresses and monthly capacities, and records the chemical products of detinning alongside national production and trade figures. It illuminates the trans-Pacific scrap-metal supply chain and Japanese concern about dependence on U.S. tinplate scrap, while also showing contemporary expectations of industrial self-sufficiency through domestic tinplate manufacture and Kyushu mining. The Singapore and Siam reference adds a regional diplomatic dimension, and the numerous cross-reference sheets—together with duplicated and inconsistently numbered pages—illustrate how economic intelligence was distributed across the State Department’s decimal filing system.
